title: Antimatter: The Universe's Disappearing Twin
summary: What if there was a twin of everything — a twin that explodes when it touches the original? That's antimatter. Every particle we know has an antimatter partner. An electron has a positron. A proton has an antiproton. They have the same mass, but opposite electric charges. When a particle meets its antimatter twin, they annihilate — they destroy each other and release a burst of energy called gamma rays. Poof! That's why antimatter is so hard to handle. You can't put it in a normal box. Scientists use magnetic and electric fields to hold it floating in mid-air, without touching anything. In March 2026, scientists at CERN did something wild: they moved antimatter in a truck for the first time. They carried antiprotons in electromagnetic fields to keep them from touching normal matter. Antimatter is super rare. A tiny bit forms when cosmic rays hit Earth's atmosphere, but it never lasts long. Scientists think the Big Bang made equal amounts of matter and antimatter. So why is our universe full of matter and almost no antimatter? That's one of the biggest mysteries in science. Maybe you'll help solve it someday!
why_it_matters: Antimatter already helps people today — hospital PET scanners use positrons — and studying it could explain how the whole universe began, a question your generation may help answer.

background_read: CERN (a huge science center in Europe where thousands of scientists study tiny particles) builds giant machines that smash particles together so scientists can see what they are made of.
Antimatter is not only in labs: hospital PET scanners use positrons to take pictures inside the human body.

The Big Bang (the enormous explosion scientists think started our universe billions of years ago) should have made equal amounts of matter and antimatter — but almost all the antimatter is gone, and nobody knows why.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists at CERN, a European particle-physics center.
WHAT: They moved antiprotons in a truck for the first time, carrying them in electromagnetic fields so the antimatter never touched ordinary matter.
WHERE: At CERN and on the road — the antimatter floated inside magnetic and electric fields instead of sitting in a normal box.
WHY: Antimatter is the key to one of science's biggest mysteries: why the universe is full of matter and almost no antimatter, even though the Big Bang should have made equal amounts of both.

perspectives.description: They call moving antimatter in a truck a first, and say it could let more labs around the world study antimatter instead of only CERN.
They warn that antimatter is extremely rare and hard to make, and one tiny touch destroys it, so moving it around is risky and expensive.
For anyone who wonders why we exist at all, the missing antimatter is a thrilling puzzle — and the article hints that a kid reading it might help solve it someday.
